claims.text: The baseline catalyst consists of Pt nanoparticles supported on conventional carbon.
The baseline Pt-on-carbon catalyst has minimal strong metal–support interaction effects.
Replacing carbon with TiO2 and applying calcination will induce strong metal–support interactions.
Strong metal–support interactions between Pt and TiO2 form interfacial Pt–TiOx bonds.
Strong metal–support interactions cause partial encapsulation of the Pt nanoparticles.
Interfacial interaction with TiO2 alters the electronic structure of Pt nanoparticles.
The altered Pt electronic structure enhances adsorption and activation of ethanol.
The altered Pt electronic structure enhances adsorption and activation of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Strong metal–support interactions reduce the propensity of Pt catalysts to become poisoned.
Enhanced intermediate activation and reduced poisoning promote complete 12-electron oxidation of ethanol.
Induced strong metal–support interactions will lower the ethanol-oxidation onset potential relative to Pt on carbon.
Induced strong metal–support interactions will increase turnover frequency relative to Pt on carbon.
Induced strong metal–support interactions will shift ethanol-oxidation products toward CO2.
Induced strong metal–support interactions will improve catalyst durability under cyclic voltammetry.
The proposed mechanism applies in acidic electrolyte when catalyst surface area and support conductivity are comparable.
Changes in pH, mass transport, or support characteristics may diminish the observable strong metal–support interaction effects.
Differences in mass transport or conductivity between TiO2- and carbon-supported catalysts may confound observed performance differences.
